screens.title: OpenShift Networking and Ingress/Egress Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will form a practical mental model of OpenShift networking and why it matters for secure, reliable clusters. OpenShift builds on Kubernetes networking primitives but adds its own software-defined networking layer — OpenShift SDN — and operational modes that control isolation and policy enforcement. You will learn three SDN modes, how Routes and Ingress resources expose services externally, how NetworkPolicy implements zero-trust controls within a project, and the two common egress strategies used to provide predictable outbound IPs. Each feature serves a distinct operational need: SDN mode determines default isolation behavior, Routes and Ingress determine how traffic enters the cluster, NetworkPolicy lets you explicitly permit or deny pod flows, and Egress Router or Egress IP lets services present stable source addresses to external systems. Throughout the chapter you'll see concrete YAML examples and a short lab workflow to deploy test applications, apply a restrictive NetworkPolicy, then open it again and simulate assigning an Egress IP. By the end you should be able to choose an SDN mode, design a NetworkPolicy that enforces least privilege, and select the right egress mechanism for firewalled external systems.

screens.title: OpenShift SDN — What it is and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: OpenShift SDN is the cluster's software-defined networking layer that provides the overlay networking and the isolation model for pods. In practice it uses Open vSwitch to implement pod networking, so pods get predictable connectivity across nodes without manual routing. Understanding SDN is essential because the chosen mode sets the baseline for project isolation and the set of network controls you can apply. For example, in a flat network pods can all talk to each other by default, meaning you'll need supplementary policies to enforce isolation. A concrete example: if your cluster uses ovs-subnet, a developer in project A can by default reach a pod in project B unless you add additional controls. A common misconception is that NetworkPolicy alone gives isolation without considering SDN mode; in reality, some SDN modes such as ovs-subnet provide no project-level isolation without NetworkPolicy or external controls. Key takeaway: SDN defines default connectivity and should be chosen to match your tenancy model. Consider whether you need enforced project isolation or prefer a flat network with more flexible policy tooling. OpenShift SDN — What it is and why it matters means openshift sdn provides the overlay network for pods and defines default isolation behavior; choose the mode to match your security needs.. In practical terms, a definition of openshift sdn and its role providing pod networking and isolation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › OpenShift SDN
OpenShift SDN — Overview
Software-defined networking that provides pod overlay and enforces default isolation model.
What it does
Implements an overlay network using Open vSwitch so pods can reach each other across nodes without manual routing.
Why it matters
SDN mode controls default project isolation and determines whether NetworkPolicy enforcement is available and meaningful.
Misconception
Some teams assume NetworkPolicy alone enforces isolation regardless of SDN mode; validate your SDN mode before relying solely on policies.
Key Takeaway

SDN sets the baseline for how pods can communicate. Pick a mode that aligns with your desired default isolation, then use NetworkPolicy for fine-grained control.

Runtime
Open vSwitch based overlay for pod traffic.

Example scenario
On a cluster running ovs-subnet a developer project could reach a payment system pod in another project unless policies or external controls restrict that traffic.

screens.title: SDN Modes: ovs-subnet, ovs-multitenant, ovs-networkpolicy
screens.narratorSegment: OpenShift provides three notable SDN modes, each with different isolation semantics. ovs-subnet offers a flat network where all pods across projects can communicate by default; it's simple but risky in multi-tenant environments because project-level isolation isn't enforced. ovs-multitenant introduces project-level isolation so pods in one project cannot reach pods in another project unless explicit allowances are made; this is useful when you want strong separation between teams. ovs-networkpolicy gives the most flexibility: it enables enforcement of Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources so you can create fine-grained allow and deny rules for pod-to-pod, namespace, or IPBlock traffic. An example contrast: if you require strict least-privilege inter-project access, ovs-multitenant or ovs-networkpolicy is preferable to ovs-subnet. A common mistake is configuring policies without understanding whether the SDN supports enforcement — a NetworkPolicy is ineffective in a mode that does not implement it. Key takeaway: select the SDN mode based on whether you need default project isolation or prefer to manage isolation via policies. SDN Modes: ovs-subnet, ovs-multitenant, ovs-networkpolicy means ovs-subnet: flat; ovs-multitenant: project isolation; ovs-networkpolicy: policy-based, granular control.. In practical terms, how each mode affects isolation and policy control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › SDN Modes
Mode comparison
Choose the SDN mode by weighing default isolation versus policy flexibility.
ovs-subnet
Flat network; pods can talk across projects by default. Simpler operations, weaker tenancy isolation.
ovs-multitenant
Project-level isolation enforced; cross-project communication blocked unless explicitly allowed.
ovs-networkpolicy
Enables Kubernetes NetworkPolicy enforcement for granular allow/deny rules.
Operational note
  • Validate the cluster's SDN mode before designing NetworkPolicies.
  • Pick ovs-multitenant or ovs-networkpolicy for multi-tenant isolation needs.
Decision aid
If you need default isolation choose ovs-multitenant. If you require precise rules and custom allowlists choose ovs-networkpolicy. If you manage a single-tenancy, ovs-subnet may suffice but review risk.
Misconception: NetworkPolicy always enforces isolation — enforcement depends on SDN support.

screens.title: Routes — exposing Services with TLS options
screens.narratorSegment: Routes are the OpenShift-native way to expose a Service using a hostname that the OpenShift Router will serve. A Route maps a host to a Service and supports TLS termination modes such as edge, passthrough, and re-encrypt. Edge termination means TLS ends at the router and traffic to the pod is unencrypted; passthrough forwards TLS to the pod for the pod to terminate; re-encrypt terminates at the router and re-encrypts to the backend. This matters when you have compliance rules requiring end-to-end TLS or when you want HAProxy-level TLS offload. Here is a typical Route YAML where termination is set to edge. Use edge when you trust internal cluster links and want the router to handle certificates. A common misconception is that Routes and Ingress are identical; Routes are OpenShift-specific and often provide router features like path or host-based rules and TLS policies more directly. Consider which termination best matches your security posture. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Routes
Route YAML walkthrough
This Route exposes a service at a hostname with TLS edge termination.
apiVersion: route.openshift.io/v1
kind: Route
metadata:
  name: my-webapp-route
spec:
  host: mywebapp.apps.example.com
  to:
    kind: Service
    name: my-webapp-service
  port:
    targetPort: 8080
  tls:
    termination: edge # TLS handled by the router
    insecureEdgeTerminationPolicy: Redirect
Edge termination
Router terminates TLS; internal traffic is unencrypted unless you re-enable TLS to backends.
Passthrough
Router passes encrypted traffic to pod for termination; useful for end-to-end TLS requirements.
Example
Use edge termination when you want the router to manage certificates centrally and you accept unencrypted cluster links.
Best practices
  • Choose termination based on compliance needs.
  • Configure health checks and failover on the external load balancer for routers.
  • When using re-encrypt, manage backend certificates carefully.
Key Takeaway
Routes are OpenShift-native and provide flexible TLS modes; pick edge, passthrough, or re-encrypt to match your security posture.

screens.title: Routes vs Ingress
screens.narratorSegment: OpenShift supports both Routes and Kubernetes Ingress resources, and the choice depends on operational needs and tooling compatibility. Routes are OpenShift-specific, exposing a Service at a host name and integrating tightly with the OpenShift Router. They typically offer direct TLS modes and routing features well suited for OpenShift-native workflows. Ingress is the Kubernetes-standard resource for HTTP(S) routing and is often used when you want compatibility with broader Kubernetes tooling or a third-party ingress controller. A concrete example: if your team uses tooling that expects Kubernetes Ingress resources and you want to reuse that stack on OpenShift, use Ingress and the Ingress Operator. Conversely, if you want the simplest OpenShift-managed routing and TLS handling, Routes are often simpler and more feature-rich in an OpenShift environment. A common misconception is that Routes are superior in all cases; they are not — choose based on ecosystem and operator expectations. Key takeaway: weigh compatibility needs against OpenShift-native router features when picking Routes or Ingress. Routes vs Ingress means use routes for openshift-native, router-managed exposure; use ingress when you need kubernetes-standard compatibility.. In practical terms, when to use openshift routes and when ingress is preferable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Routes vs Ingress
Routes and Ingress — a practical comparison
Routes (OpenShift)
  • OpenShift-native; integrates with OpenShift Router.
  • Supports TLS termination modes directly: edge, passthrough, re-encrypt.
  • Simpler for OpenShift-focused workflows.
Ingress (Kubernetes)
  • Standard Kubernetes resource; portable across clusters.
  • Use when external tooling expects Ingress resources or a custom controller is required.
  • Managed by the Ingress Operator on OpenShift when installed.
Example decision
If your CI/CD pipelines create Ingress resources and you rely on that ecosystem, prefer Ingress. If you want router-managed TLS and simpler OpenShift UX, prefer Routes.

screens.title: NetworkPolicy fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: NetworkPolicy is a Kubernetes resource that defines rules controlling how groups of pods communicate with each other and with external endpoints. By default, pods are non-isolated and can talk freely; creating a NetworkPolicy allows you to restrict traffic so only permitted sources or destinations are allowed. A NetworkPolicy can select pods by label, specify ingress and egress rules, and use namespaceSelector or ipBlock to define sources. For example, a policy can allow only pods labeled 'frontend' to reach pods labeled 'backend' on TCP port 8080. A common pitfall is creating a policy that unintentionally blocks health checks or cluster infrastructure traffic because the default deny semantics can cut off necessary flows. Always test policies in staging: apply a deny-all and then add explicit allow rules for required services, monitoring, and DNS. Key takeaway: use NetworkPolicy to implement least privilege for pod communication, but validate each policy's side effects before applying in production. NetworkPolicy fundamentals means networkpolicy enables explicit allow/deny rules for pods; start with deny-all in staging and add minimal required allowances.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › NetworkPolicy
NetworkPolicy basics
Define pod selectors and ingress/egress rules to enforce least privilege.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend-to-backend
  namespace: my-app-project
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress
  ingress:
    - from:
      - podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: frontend
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
  egress:
    - to:
      - ipBlock:
          cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443
Practical tip
Test by applying a restrictive policy in staging, verify critical services such as DNS and monitoring still work, then tighten rules incrementally.
Common mistakes
  • Applying deny-all without explicit allows for cluster DNS or health checks.
  • Assuming a policy works across namespaces without namespaceSelector.
Key Takeaway
NetworkPolicy is powerful but must be tested carefully. Use labels and namespace selectors to write precise rules and avoid accidental outages.

screens.title: Lab: deploy frontend & backend and verify connectivity
screens.narratorSegment: This lab walkthrough guides you through deploying two simple Nginx applications, confirming connectivity, applying a deny-all NetworkPolicy to the backend, and then verifying that traffic is blocked. Start by creating a new project and applying the frontend and backend deployments and services. After the pods are running, get the backend service cluster IP and use oc exec into the frontend pod to curl the backend service — you should receive the Nginx welcome H T M L. Next, apply a 'deny-all' NetworkPolicy that selects backend pods and sets ingress to an empty list; this denies all ingress to those pods. Re-run the same curl from the frontend pod; the request should time out or fail, demonstrating that the policy is effective. Finally, update the NetworkPolicy to allow traffic explicitly from the frontend pod selector and port 8080 and verify connectivity is restored. A common mistake is forgetting to allow DNS or other system traffic; ensure you only deny what is safe to deny in staging. narration.text: This lab walkthrough guides you through deploying two simple Nginx applications, confirming connectivity, applying a deny-all NetworkPolicy to the backend, and then verifying that traffic is blocked. Start by creating a new project and applying the frontend and backend deployments and services. After the pods are running, get the backend service cluster IP and use oc exec into the frontend pod to curl the backend service — you should receive the Nginx welcome H T M L. Next, apply a 'deny-all' NetworkPolicy that selects backend pods and sets ingress to an empty list; this denies all ingress to those pods. Re-run the same curl from the frontend pod; the request should time out or fail, demonstrating that the policy is effective. Finally, update the NetworkPolicy to allow traffic explicitly from the frontend pod selector and port 8080 and verify connectivity is restored. A common mistake is forgetting to allow DNS or other system traffic; ensure you only deny what is safe to deny in staging. The closing question: when the deny-all is in place, which other services should you verify still have access?

Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Lab Walkthrough
Terminal actions
Run these commands to deploy and verify connectivity.
# create project and deploy
oc login --token=<your_token> --server=<your_api_url>
oc new-project network-test-project
oc apply -f frontend-deployment.yaml -f frontend-service.yaml -f backend-deployment.yaml -f backend-service.yaml -n network-test-project

# verify connectivity from frontend pod
FRONTEND_POD=$(oc get pod -l app=frontend -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}' -n network-test-project)
oc exec $FRONTEND_POD -n network-test-project -- curl -s http://backend-service.network-test-project.svc.cluster.local:8080
Apply deny-all
# backend-network-policy.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all-to-backend
  namespace: network-test-project
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress: []
Observations and checks
  • Before policy: curl returns Nginx HTML.
  • After deny-all: curl times out or returns connection error.
  • After allowing frontend selector: connectivity returns.
Common pitfall
Don't forget to permit DNS and cluster services if your workload depends on them; otherwise you may block necessary system traffic.

screens.title: Updating NetworkPolicy to allow frontend → backend traffic
screens.narratorSegment: After demonstrating that a deny-all policy blocks traffic, the next step is to update the NetworkPolicy to permit traffic only from the frontend. This enforces least privilege while restoring required connectivity. The updated policy selects backend pods and adds an ingress rule that allows pods with label 'app: frontend' to connect to TCP port 8080. Apply the new YAML and re-run the curl from the frontend pod; you should receive the Nginx response again. When crafting these rules, be careful to include any auxiliary flows such as health probes, monitoring, or DNS. A common misconception is that adding a single allow rule is always enough; in clusters with sidecars or service meshes you may need additional selectors or egress rules. Key takeaway: incrementally add explicit allows until functionality is restored, and keep tests simple — a curl from a test pod is the fastest verification. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Allow frontend
Allow frontend → backend (YAML)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-frontend-to-backend
  namespace: network-test-project
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
      - podSelector:
          matchLabels:
            app: frontend
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
Apply this policy with oc apply -f and then re-run the curl from the frontend pod to confirm the response is restored.
Verification
# get frontend pod
FRONTEND_POD=$(oc get pod -l app=frontend -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}' -n network-test-project)
# test
oc exec $FRONTEND_POD -n network-test-project -- curl -s http://backend-service.network-test-project.svc.cluster.local:8080
Key Takeaway
Apply minimal allow rules and iterate. Always confirm DNS, health checks, and monitoring traffic remain accessible after changes.

screens.title: Egress Router and Egress IP — predictable outbound addresses
screens.narratorSegment: OpenShift offers two common approaches to control outbound source IP: Egress Router and Egress IP. An Egress Router is a pod that forwards outbound traffic for a project through a specific instance, which can be configured with a dedicated IP. This lets applications present a consistent source IP to external systems and also centralizes outbound traffic for inspection or NAT. Egress IP assigns a static, dedicated IP address to a project or selected pods so their outbound traffic is source-NATed to that IP. Egress IP tends to be simpler when you only need a static source address because it requires fewer moving parts than routing through a proxy pod. A concrete example: integrate with a legacy firewall that only allows a fixed source IP — assign an Egress IP to the project so connections use that address. A common misconception is that Egress Router and Egress IP are interchangeable without operational differences; in practice, Egress Router requires managing the router pod, while Egress IP relies on cluster network support and available addresses. Key takeaway: choose Egress IP for simplicity when supported, and Egress Router when you need more control over outbound processing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Egress Strategies
Egress Router
Traffic originates from pods in a project and is routed through a designated router pod which can have a specific IP.
Use when you need granular control over outbound processing, logging, or when source IP isn't easily assigned by the cluster network.
Egress IP
Assigns a static source IP to pods or a project; outbound traffic is SNATed to that IP by the cluster network.
Simpler for firewall scenarios where only a fixed source IP is required and the cluster supports egress IPs on nodes.
Example commands (simulation)
# annotate namespace to assign egress IPs (example)
oc patch namespace network-test-project -p '{"metadata": {"annotations": {"network.openshift.io/assign-egress-ips": "true"}}}' --type=merge
# or add egress IP (cluster-admin action)
oc adm egress-ip add-ip 192.168.1.100 --selector=app=frontend -n network-test-project

screens.title: Simulate assigning an Egress IP (lab guidance)
screens.narratorSegment: Assigning an Egress IP typically requires cluster-admin privileges and depends on your cluster network configuration. In a lab, you can simulate the assignment and verify the outbound source IP by checking pod annotations or by making an outbound request to a test endpoint that returns the source address. The general steps are: enable egress IPs on the namespace via an annotation if your cluster requires that, or use the cluster admin command to assign the IP to a selector. For example, adding an annotation to the namespace requests the cluster to support project egress assignment; then you either patch the deployment or use oc adm commands to attach the IP. After assignment, verify with oc get egressip or oc get pod -o wide to confirm the IP appears. Finally, make an outbound curl from the pod to an external endpoint that echoes the source IP; you should observe the assigned Egress IP. A common pitfall is assuming the IP is immediately available — node-level routing and address availability must be confirmed. Key question: which verification steps would you run first to confirm the Egress IP is active?

Simulate Egress IP assignment

Example steps

screens.title: Troubleshooting OpenShift networking
screens.narratorSegment: When a network problem occurs, follow a disciplined checklist to narrow the cause quickly. Start with DNS resolution — confirm the service name resolves and that CoreDNS is functional. Next, check NetworkPolicies in the namespace; an overly restrictive policy is a common root cause. Then verify Service configuration: is the Service selecting the correct pod labels and exposing the right port? Check Routes and Ingress to ensure hostnames and TLS are configured properly. Finally, validate pod-level connectivity by using oc exec into a pod and running ping or curl to the target. Use pod logs and describe to surface any container or readiness probe errors that affect routing. A concrete troubleshooting example: a curl from frontend to backend fails — first check that the backend service clusterIP exists and points to running endpoints, then inspect any NetworkPolicy that might deny ingress. A common misconception is to blame routers or external load balancers first; often the issue is an internal Service selector, label mismatch, or a NetworkPolicy. Key takeaway: work from DNS and policies through services and routes, using simple pod exec checks to confirm each layer.

Systematic checks to find the source of networking issues.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will form a practical mental model of OpenShift networking and why it matters for secure, reliable clusters. OpenShift builds on Kubernetes networking primitives but adds its own software-defined networking layer — OpenShift SDN — and operational modes that control isolation and policy enforcement. You will learn three SDN modes, how Routes and Ingress resources expose services externally, how NetworkPolicy implements zero-trust controls within a project, and the two common egress strategies used to provide predictable outbound IPs. Each feature serves a distinct operational need: SDN mode determines default isolation behavior, Routes and Ingress determine how traffic enters the cluster, NetworkPolicy lets you explicitly permit or deny pod flows, and Egress Router or Egress IP lets services present stable source addresses to external systems. Throughout the chapter you'll see concrete YAML examples and a short lab workflow to deploy test applications, apply a restrictive NetworkPolicy, then open it again and simulate assigning an Egress IP. By the end you should be able to choose an SDN mode, design a NetworkPolicy that enforces least privilege, and select the right egress mechanism for firewalled external systems.

In these objectives I'll map the chapter goals to practical competencies you can verify. First, you'll deepen your operational knowledge of OpenShift SDN modes — you should be able to explain differences between ovs-subnet, ovs-multitenant, and ovs-networkpolicy and the security implications of each. Second, you'll configure Routes and Ingress so applications are reachable externally with the correct TLS termination mode. Third, you'll author and apply NetworkPolicies to restrict pod-to-pod traffic precisely, and understand how to test policies using simple curl checks. Fourth, you'll explore egress techniques, including assigning an Egress IP or using an Egress Router so pods present a stable source IP to firewalled systems. Each objective includes a competency milestone you can verify in a lab: deploy test apps, apply a policy that blocks and then allows traffic, and simulate assigning an Egress IP. These skills matter because networking is where many production outages and security gaps appear; being able to reason about SDN modes, exposure resources, and egress guarantees helps you design resilient and compliant clusters.

This screen links each learning objective to a lab action and an assessment check. For SDN modes, your lab step is to identify which mode the cluster runs in and reason about whether project isolation is sufficient; the assessment asks you to explain a scenario where ovs-subnet is risky. For Routes and Ingress, the lab will create a Route with TLS edge termination and confirm access; the assessment will ask you to choose termination modes for given compliance constraints. For NetworkPolicy, the lab actions are to apply a deny-all policy, verify broken connectivity, then allow a specific frontend pod selector and re-verify. The assessment will ask you to write a NetworkPolicy that allows only an 'api-gateway' namespace to reach 'database' pods. For egress, the lab puts you through simulating an Egress IP assignment and verifying source IP from an external test endpoint; the assessment will ask which feature best satisfies a firewall that requires a fixed source IP. Each mapping reinforces the objective by making it verifiable in a cluster environment.

OpenShift SDN is the cluster's software-defined networking layer that provides the overlay networking and the isolation model for pods. In practice it uses Open vSwitch to implement pod networking, so pods get predictable connectivity across nodes without manual routing. Understanding SDN is essential because the chosen mode sets the baseline for project isolation and the set of network controls you can apply. For example, in a flat network pods can all talk to each other by default, meaning you'll need supplementary policies to enforce isolation. A concrete example: if your cluster uses ovs-subnet, a developer in project A can by default reach a pod in project B unless you add additional controls. A common misconception is that NetworkPolicy alone gives isolation without considering SDN mode; in reality, some SDN modes such as ovs-subnet provide no project-level isolation without NetworkPolicy or external controls. Key takeaway: SDN defines default connectivity and should be chosen to match your tenancy model. Consider whether you need enforced project isolation or prefer a flat network with more flexible policy tooling. OpenShift SDN — What it is and why it matters means openshift sdn provides the overlay network for pods and defines default isolation behavior; choose the mode to match your security needs.. In practical terms, a definition of openshift sdn and its role providing pod networking and isolation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

OpenShift provides three notable SDN modes, each with different isolation semantics. ovs-subnet offers a flat network where all pods across projects can communicate by default; it's simple but risky in multi-tenant environments because project-level isolation isn't enforced. ovs-multitenant introduces project-level isolation so pods in one project cannot reach pods in another project unless explicit allowances are made; this is useful when you want strong separation between teams. ovs-networkpolicy gives the most flexibility: it enables enforcement of Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources so you can create fine-grained allow and deny rules for pod-to-pod, namespace, or IPBlock traffic. An example contrast: if you require strict least-privilege inter-project access, ovs-multitenant or ovs-networkpolicy is preferable to ovs-subnet. A common mistake is configuring policies without understanding whether the SDN supports enforcement — a NetworkPolicy is ineffective in a mode that does not implement it. Key takeaway: select the SDN mode based on whether you need default project isolation or prefer to manage isolation via policies. SDN Modes: ovs-subnet, ovs-multitenant, ovs-networkpolicy means ovs-subnet: flat; ovs-multitenant: project isolation; ovs-networkpolicy: policy-based, granular control.. In practical terms, how each mode affects isolation and policy control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Routes are the OpenShift-native way to expose a Service using a hostname that the OpenShift Router will serve. A Route maps a host to a Service and supports TLS termination modes such as edge, passthrough, and re-encrypt. Edge termination means TLS ends at the router and traffic to the pod is unencrypted; passthrough forwards TLS to the pod for the pod to terminate; re-encrypt terminates at the router and re-encrypts to the backend. This matters when you have compliance rules requiring end-to-end TLS or when you want HAProxy-level TLS offload. Here is a typical Route YAML where termination is set to edge. Use edge when you trust internal cluster links and want the router to handle certificates. A common misconception is that Routes and Ingress are identical; Routes are OpenShift-specific and often provide router features like path or host-based rules and TLS policies more directly. Consider which termination best matches your security posture. Routes — exposing Services with TLS options means routes let openshift router expose services at a hostname and support edge, passthrough, and re-encrypt tls options.. In practical terms, route resource yaml and tls termination modes explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

OpenShift supports both Routes and Kubernetes Ingress resources, and the choice depends on operational needs and tooling compatibility. Routes are OpenShift-specific, exposing a Service at a host name and integrating tightly with the OpenShift Router. They typically offer direct TLS modes and routing features well suited for OpenShift-native workflows. Ingress is the Kubernetes-standard resource for HTTP(S) routing and is often used when you want compatibility with broader Kubernetes tooling or a third-party ingress controller. A concrete example: if your team uses tooling that expects Kubernetes Ingress resources and you want to reuse that stack on OpenShift, use Ingress and the Ingress Operator. Conversely, if you want the simplest OpenShift-managed routing and TLS handling, Routes are often simpler and more feature-rich in an OpenShift environment. A common misconception is that Routes are superior in all cases; they are not — choose based on ecosystem and operator expectations. Key takeaway: weigh compatibility needs against OpenShift-native router features when picking Routes or Ingress. Routes vs Ingress means use routes for openshift-native, router-managed exposure; use ingress when you need kubernetes-standard compatibility.. In practical terms, when to use openshift routes and when ingress is preferable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

NetworkPolicy is a Kubernetes resource that defines rules controlling how groups of pods communicate with each other and with external endpoints. By default, pods are non-isolated and can talk freely; creating a NetworkPolicy allows you to restrict traffic so only permitted sources or destinations are allowed. A NetworkPolicy can select pods by label, specify ingress and egress rules, and use namespaceSelector or ipBlock to define sources. For example, a policy can allow only pods labeled 'frontend' to reach pods labeled 'backend' on TCP port 8080. A common pitfall is creating a policy that unintentionally blocks health checks or cluster infrastructure traffic because the default deny semantics can cut off necessary flows. Always test policies in staging: apply a deny-all and then add explicit allow rules for required services, monitoring, and DNS. OpenShift offers two common approaches to control outbound source IP: Egress Router and Egress IP. An Egress Router is a pod that forwards outbound traffic for a project through a specific instance, which can be configured with a dedicated IP. This lets applications present a consistent source IP to external systems and also centralizes outbound traffic for inspection or NAT. Egress IP assigns a static, dedicated IP address to a project or selected pods so their outbound traffic is source-NATed to that IP. Egress IP tends to be simpler when you only need a static source address because it requires fewer moving parts than routing through a proxy pod. A concrete example: integrate with a legacy firewall that only allows a fixed source IP — assign an Egress IP to the project so connections use that address. A common misconception is that Egress Router and Egress IP are interchangeable without operational differences; in practice, Egress Router requires managing the router pod, while Egress IP relies on cluster network support and available addresses. Key takeaway: choose Egress IP for simplicity when supported, and Egress Router when you need more control over outbound processing.

Assigning an Egress IP typically requires cluster-admin privileges and depends on your cluster network configuration. In a lab, you can simulate the assignment and verify the outbound source IP by checking pod annotations or by making an outbound request to a test endpoint that returns the source address. The general steps are: enable egress IPs on the namespace via an annotation if your cluster requires that, or use the cluster admin command to assign the IP to a selector. For example, adding an annotation to the namespace requests the cluster to support project egress assignment; then you either patch the deployment or use oc adm commands to attach the IP. After assignment, verify with oc get egressip or oc get pod -o wide to confirm the IP appears. Finally, make an outbound curl from the pod to an external endpoint that echoes the source IP; you should observe the assigned Egress IP. A common pitfall is assuming the IP is immediately available — node-level routing and address availability must be confirmed. Key question: which verification steps would you run first to confirm the Egress IP is active?

When a network problem occurs, follow a disciplined checklist to narrow the cause quickly. Start with DNS resolution — confirm the service name resolves and that CoreDNS is functional. Next, check NetworkPolicies in the namespace; an overly restrictive policy is a common root cause. Then verify Service configuration: is the Service selecting the correct pod labels and exposing the right port? Check Routes and Ingress to ensure hostnames and TLS are configured properly. Finally, validate pod-level connectivity by using oc exec into a pod and running ping or curl to the target. Use pod logs and describe to surface any container or readiness probe errors that affect routing. A concrete troubleshooting example: a curl from frontend to backend fails — first check that the backend service clusterIP exists and points to running endpoints, then inspect any NetworkPolicy that might deny ingress. A common misconception is to blame routers or external load balancers first; often the issue is an internal Service selector, label mismatch, or a NetworkPolicy. Key takeaway: work from DNS and policies through services and routes, using simple pod exec checks to confirm each layer.

Let's close by reinforcing three core concepts you should carry forward. First, OpenShift SDN determines default connectivity and isolation; choose the mode that fits your tenancy and security model. Second, Routes are the native OpenShift way to expose Services with built-in TLS modes, while Ingress provides Kubernetes-standard compatibility; select based on your operational ecosystem. Third, NetworkPolicy is the mechanism for least-privilege pod-to-pod controls, but its effectiveness depends on SDN mode and careful testing. These three ideas interlock: pick an SDN mode, use Routes/Ingress for external exposure, and apply NetworkPolicy to lock down internal traffic. As a final reflective question: which SDN mode and egress strategy would you choose for a multi-tenant cluster that must present a fixed IP to an external partner?
